# FDG8026

> DO NOT return null values from collection properties or from methods returning collections. Return an empty collection or an empty array instead.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 8.3.2 Collection Properties and Return Values.

## How it is checked

- Check: fdg (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: FDG8026
- Automatic fix: no
- Severity: library warning, application warning, test warning
- Status: verified

Message: Return an empty collection instead of null from '{0}'

FDG8026 reports a null or default literal, directly, through a conversion or as a branch of a conditional expression, returned by a method, local function, property getter or indexer getter as an array or a collection: IEnumerable, IEnumerable<T>, or a type that implements ICollection, ICollection<T> or IReadOnlyCollection<T> and is, or derives from, a type of the System.Collections namespaces (List<T>, IList<T>, Collection<T> and the immutable and concurrent collections are). The type is the one the value is converted to, which is the T of the Task<T> of an async method. Types that are only enumerable, such as XmlNode, and other types that implement the collection interfaces, such as the nodes of a document tree, are not checked: they are not collections first, and null is a usual value for them (noise samples, see docs/noise-samples.md). A collection type that implements the interfaces without deriving from a System.Collections type is missed. Lambdas and anonymous methods are not checked. Null values computed elsewhere (a field, a call) are not seen, so coverage is partial. Returning an empty collection changes no signature, but there is no code fix.

## From the book

Users of collection properties often assume that the following code will always work:

```csharp
IEnumerable<string> list = GetList();
foreach(string name in list){
  ...
}
```

The general rule is that null and empty (zero-item) collections or arrays should be treated the same.
